docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This page shows the electrical architecture of my subsystem for Team 102's Modular Spider Leg. In the team's hub-and-spoke layout, my board is the spoke on hub connector 3. It drives the leg's small linear actuator (the actuator) and measures leg motion with an accelerometer for jerk and impulse sensing (the sensor). Commands come from Preston's hub board over the ribbon cable.

The design follows the RAS 304 project requirements:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the microcontroller.
  • A 9 V barrel jack feeding a 5 V linear regulator, with a fuse and a power-status LED.
  • A 2x4 male IDC header using the class ribbon pinout.
  • No daughter boards: every peripheral, including the accelerometer, is placed directly on this PCB.

Parts were also chosen to stay within the team's $70–80 total budget.

The block diagram shows:

  • Power levels: my own 9 V adapter → barrel jack → fuse → L7805 linear regulator (5 V) for the motor driver, the actuator motor, and the Curiosity Nano. The Curiosity Nano's on-board regulator supplies 3.3 V to the accelerometer and the position potentiometer.
  • Actuator: an N20 gear motor with an M3 lead screw, driven by a TI DRV8833 H-bridge. A current-sense resistor allows stall detection.
  • Position feedback: a Bourns slide potentiometer whose slider moves with the actuator's lead-screw nut.
  • Sensor: an ST LIS3DH 3-axis accelerometer chip on SPI, with a data-ready interrupt.
  • Team connection: an 8-pin ribbon cable to Preston's hub board. It carries position commands in and jerk/impulse data out over UART.

docs.title: Team Connection
docs.text:
My board connects to Preston's hub board (Leg Kinematics) through hub connector 3, using the class-standard 8-pin ribbon cable and a 2x4 male IDC header. The ribbon carries signals and a shared ground only; my board is powered by its own 9 V adapter.

Pin Type Signal Direction MCU Pin 1 Digital UART RX: position commands from the hub Hub → my board RC7 (U1RX) 2 Digital UART TX: jerk / impulse data to the hub My board → hub RC6 (U1TX) 3–5 Digital Not used — — 6–7 Analog Not used — — 8 GND Common ground — GND

docs.title: Design Notes
docs.text:
• Closed-loop position control: the hub sends a target position over UART. The PIC compares it with the slide-pot reading on RA1, then drives the two PWM outputs (RC2, RD0) to move the lead screw forward or back.
  • Stall and fault protection (Req. 6.1): current through the DRV8833 flows through a 0.3 Ω sense resistor on AISEN. The PIC reads that voltage on RA0 and stops the motor if the current stays high, which indicates a stall. The same resistor also sets the driver's built-in current limit at about 0.67 A (0.2 V ÷ 0.3 Ω), which keeps a motor fault within what my 1 A adapter can supply. The nFAULT pin (RB1) reports over-current or over-temperature, and the PIC then disables the driver through nSLEEP (RD1).
  • Jerk and impulse sensing: the LIS3DH data-ready interrupt (RB0) triggers an SPI read of acceleration at up to about 1.3 kHz. Jerk is found by differentiating acceleration, and impulse by integrating force (mass × acceleration) over the foot-contact time. The results are sent to the hub over UART.
  • Accelerometer soldering: the LIS3DHTR is a 3 × 3 mm LGA-16 package. Because daughter boards aren't allowed, it is soldered directly to the PCB with a stencil and hot air or reflow.
  • Speed vs. cost: a standard M3 lead screw moves 0.5 mm per turn, so the 98 RPM (60 RPM under load) FIT0577 gives about 0.5–0.8 mm/s. That is slow, but adequate for a small demonstration leg, and much cheaper than a commercial linear actuator with built-in feedback (about $80 or more).

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
RAS 304 – Individual Datasheet (Kaushik) – Driver Nano 3: Linear Actuator B + IMU Project: Team 102 Modular Spider Leg (my board is the spoke on hub connector 3)

Scope: this page covers only my individual board (Driver Nano 3). Team-level decisions are in the team repository. The selected part types are the same ones shown on my Block Diagram page. Every product link below goes to a supplier that sells to customers in the United States, and prices are US dollar prices for quantity 1 checked on 2026-10-19 (they will change, and shipping and tax are not included).

docs.title: 1. Subsystem summary
docs.text:
Driver Nano 3 handles Linear Actuator B control and IMU sensing. It follows this loop from the team software flow diagram:

  1. Receive the actuator B target position from the Main Processor (Preston's hub board).
  2. Drive Linear Actuator B (PWM and direction).
  3. Read the IMU orientation (I2C / SPI).
  4. Check whether the orientation is within the expected range. If yes, continue the motion. If no, adjust the motion or flag a status.
  5. Send actuator B status and IMU data back to the Main Processor.
  6. Loop, waiting for the next command.

When the Main Processor sends a stop command, Driver Nano 3 disables the driver and reports a safe status. The Main Processor does the kinematics; my board only runs local control and returns feedback continuously. The team calls the sensor output "jerk / impulse" data, which the PIC computes from the accelerometer readings.

Budget constraint: the whole team budget is $70 to $80 for four boards, so each board should cost about $17.50 to $20.00. That limits every choice below, especially the actuator.

Other project constraints:

  • PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano as the MCU. Its I/O and ADC run at its target voltage, 3.3 V as shipped (Curiosity Nano user guide, section 3.3.1).
  • External 9 V barrel-jack adapter, 5 V linear regulator, fuse and power indicator.
  • No daughter boards: the IMU is a bare chip on my PCB.

docs.title: 2.1 [Actuator B subsystem] Linear actuator
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. DFRobot Micro Metal DC Geared Motor with Lead Screw (FIT0577), 6 V, 98 RPM, M3 × 20 mm$9.00 each ($11.76 at RobotShop)DFRobot product page · RobotShop listing • Same design as my Block Diagram choice: an N20 6 V gearmotor with the M3 lead screw built onto the shaft• Ready-made part that can be ordered in the US (DFRobot, or RobotShop's US store)• Published electrical data: 24 mA no load and 420 mA stall at 6 V, so the power budget is based on real numbers• $9.00 fits the board's share of the team budget• Rated 6 V, so it runs from the 5 V rail through the DRV8833 • Slow: 98 RPM no load and 60 RPM under load, which is about 0.5 to 0.8 mm/s with a standard 0.5 mm M3 pitch (the page does not state the pitch)• The 20 mm screw limits the stroke to under 20 mm• No built-in position feedback, so it needs the slide potentiometer• Shipping cost and time are not included Option 2. Aslong N20 6 V 300 RPM gearmotor (3 mm shaft) plus an M3 threaded rod and shaft coupler$6.95 for the motor; rod and coupler not pricedRobotShop product page • 300 RPM, about three times the speed of Option 1 (about 2.5 mm/s with a 0.5 mm pitch)• Lowest price for the motor itself• Rated 6 V, all-metal gears• Longer screw possible, so more stroke • Sold as a plain gearmotor, so the lead screw, a coupler or adapter between the 3 mm shaft and the screw, and a nut must be sourced and aligned• Extra cost and mechanical work that is not in the $6.95 price• The page lists no stall current or torque, so the power budget would rest on an estimate• More risk of misalignment and backlash Option 3. Pololu 298:1 Micro Metal Gearmotor LP 6 V (plain gearmotor, no lead screw)$23.95 eachPololu product page • Published specs: 40 mA no load, 0.36 A stall (extrapolated), 2.0 kg·cm stall torque• High quality and well documented• Strong for its size • $23.95 for the motor alone, already above a whole board's budget share• Needs a separate lead screw and coupling, which adds cost and mechanical work• Only 45 RPM no load, very slow Option 4. Actuonix PQ12-P 6 V, 20 mm, 100:1, potentiometer feedback$81.76 eachRobotShop product page · PQ12 datasheet • Complete actuator with built-in 5 kΩ position potentiometer• 40 N peak force at 6 mm/s, 550 mA stall at 6 V• Well documented • $81.76 is more than the entire $70 to $80 team budget• 20% maximum duty cycle• Potentiometer tolerance of ±50% needs calibration

Choice: Option 1, DFRobot FIT0577 N20 gearmotor with M3 lead screw [Actuator B subsystem]

Rationale: The team budget is $70 to $80 for four boards, so my board has about $17.50 to $20.00 to spend in total, and the actuator must also be orderable in the US. Option 1 keeps the design from my Block Diagram page (an N20 6 V gearmotor driving an M3 lead screw) as one ready-made part, costs $9.00, and comes with published stall and no-load currents. Option 2 gives the original 300 RPM speed for a little less money, but it leaves me to buy and align the screw and coupler, and it has no published current data. The Pololu motor alone ($23.95) is more than the board's whole share, and the commercial actuator costs more than the entire team budget. I accept the slow speed (a joint demonstration does not need fast motion) and the missing feedback (covered by the slide potentiometer in 2.3). If the team needs more speed later, Option 2 is the fallback.

docs.title: 2.2 [Actuator B subsystem] Motor driver (H-bridge)
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. TI DRV8833PWPR dual H-bridge, HTSSOP-16 with PowerPAD$3.02 each (Digi-Key and Mouser)Digi-Key product page · TI datasheet • MOSFET bridge: only about 0.36 Ω total on-resistance at 5 V, so about 0.2 V is lost at 0.6 A and the motor sees nearly the full 5 V• 2.7 to 10.8 V motor supply, 1.5 A RMS and 2 A peak per bridge, plenty of margin over a small N20• Adjustable current limit with one sense resistor (0.2 V ÷ R), which also gives stall detection• nFAULT output, nSLEEP pin and thermal shutdown• Logic threshold of 2 V (2.5 V on nSLEEP) works with the Nano's 3.3 V outputs• Very low sleep current• Lowest cost of the three options • Surface-mount only: 5.0 × 4.4 mm package with an exposed pad, which needs hot air or reflow to solder properly• No built-in current sense output, so an external sense resistor and ADC reading are needed• Dissipation goes through the exposed pad, so the PCB needs a copper pour under it Option 2. TI SN754410NE quadruple half-H driver, DIP-16$4.50 eachSparkFun product page · TI datasheet • Through-hole DIP, easiest to solder and replace• 1 A continuous per channel, built-in clamp diodes• Thermal shutdown • Bipolar outputs lose roughly 2.6 to 3.6 V in total near 0.6 A, so on a 5 V rail a 6 V motor would see only about 1.5 to 2.5 V and barely turn• No current limit or fault output• About 1.5 times the cost of the DRV8833• Large quiescent supply current Option 3. L293D dual H-bridge, DIP-16$8.95 each (price as listed)Adafruit product page · TI datasheet • Through-hole DIP, well documented, many examples• Internal kickback diodes • Same bipolar voltage-drop problem as Option 2, so the 6 V motor is starved on 5 V• Only 600 mA continuous, with no margin against stall• Most expensive option and no fault or current-limit features

Choice: Option 1, DRV8833PWPR [Actuator B subsystem]

Rationale: The motor is fed from the 5 V rail, so the driver must drop almost nothing. Only the MOSFET-based DRV8833 does that; the bipolar DIP drivers would waste about half of the available voltage. It is also the lowest-cost option, has a built-in current limit and fault output that give me stall detection and protection (a project requirement), and works directly from the Nano's 3.3 V signals. The cost is a harder soldering job, which I accept with a stencil and hot air or reflow, and a copper pour under the exposed pad.

docs.title: 2.3 [Actuator B subsystem] Position sensor for the lead-screw nut
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. Bourns PTA2043-2015CPB103 slide potentiometer, 10 kΩ, 20 mm travel$1.84 each (Newark and Avnet)Digi-Key product page • Gives an absolute position reading directly on one ADC pin• Through-hole, simple to mount• Very inexpensive• Slider can be coupled to the lead-screw nut for closed-loop control• Runs from the Nano's 3.3 V rail, so the signal stays within the ADC range • Only 20 mm of travel, which limits the usable stroke• ±20% resistance tolerance, so each unit needs calibration• Mechanical wear and slider noise over time• Needs a mechanical link between the slider and the nut Option 2. Bourns PTA4543-2015DPB103 slide potentiometer, 10 kΩ, 45 mm travel$2.21 each (Avnet), $2.35 (Newark)Digi-Key product page • 45 mm of travel allows a longer stroke• Same signal type and ADC interface as Option 1• Still inexpensive • Larger body is hard to fit on a small leg• Travel is longer than the short N20 stroke needs, so resolution per millimetre of actuator motion is lower• Same tolerance and wear limits as Option 1 Option 3 (custom). Two end-stop microswitches plus motor-current stall detectionNo single commercial part; cost is low but not yet quoted • No sensing part on the leg beyond the switches• Uses the sense resistor already in the design • Only end positions are known, so there is no continuous position, which breaks closed-loop control• Position between the stops would be estimated from time, which drifts• Does not meet the software flow's position control

Choice: Option 1, PTA2043-2015CPB103 [Actuator B subsystem]

Rationale: The software flow needs continuous position control, and the potentiometer is the lowest-cost way to get an absolute position on a single ADC pin. The 20 mm travel suits a small joint, and the slider can ride on the lead-screw nut. I accept the tolerance and wear limits and will calibrate each unit in firmware.

docs.title: 2.4 [IMU subsystem] Accelerometer / IMU
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. ST LIS3DHTR 3-axis accelerometer, LGA-16 (3 × 3 mm)$1.94 each (Newark and Avnet)Digi-Key product page · ST datasheet • Lowest cost of the sensors that fit the budget• 1.71 to 3.6 V supply, so it runs from the Nano's 3.3 V• SPI and I2C, and selectable ±2, ±4, ±8 and ±16 g ranges• Data-ready interrupt lets the PIC read samples only when new data exist• Gravity vector gives roll and pitch for the "orientation within range" check• Fast enough to estimate jerk and impulse • 3 × 3 mm LGA is hard to solder by hand and needs a stencil and hot air or reflow• Accelerometer only, so no gyroscope and no yaw• Jerk must be computed in firmware by differentiating the samples Option 2. Analog Devices ADXL345BCCZ 3-axis accelerometer, LGA-14 (3 × 5 mm)$8.66 each at Newark ($7.05 at Arrow, $10.36 at Mouser)Digi-Key product page · Analog Devices datasheet • ±16 g range with SPI and I2C• 2 to 3.6 V supply, works from 3.3 V• Built-in shock/tap and activity detection, useful for impulse events• Well documented • About four times the price of the LIS3DH, using a large part of the board's budget share• Larger 3 × 5 mm LGA is still hard to solder• Still no gyroscope Option 3. TDK InvenSense MPU-6050 6-axis IMU, QFN-24 (4 × 4 mm)US price not confirmed (I found $5.78 at one reseller and $20.99 at LCSC)Digi-Key product page · InvenSense datasheet • Adds a 3-axis gyroscope for true orientation• I2C interface, 2.375 to 3.46 V supply • Even at the lowest price I found it is about three times the cost of the LIS3DH, and the price varies widely between sellers• I2C only• 4 × 4 mm QFN with an exposed pad is the hardest to solder• More capability than the jerk and impulse sensing needs

Choice: Option 1, LIS3DHTR [IMU subsystem]

Rationale: The team assigned my board jerk and impulse sensing, which only needs acceleration, and the orientation check in the software flow can be done from the gravity vector. The LIS3DH is the lowest-cost option, runs from the Nano's 3.3 V rail, supports SPI with a data-ready interrupt, and fits the budget. The other two cost at least about three to four times as much for features (gyroscope, built-in tap detection) the task does not require. The soldering risk (3 × 3 mm LGA) is accepted and handled with a stencil and hot air or reflow; this is the same risk any of the three options carries.

docs.title: 2.5 [Power subsystem] 5 V linear voltage regulator
docs.text:
Solution Pros Cons Option 1. ST L7805CV 5 V regulator, TO-220$0.65 eachJameco product page · ST datasheet • Up to 1.5 A with internal current limiting and thermal shutdown• Specified for 7 to 18 V input, which brackets the 9 V adapter• Output capacitor is not needed for stability• Very inexpensive and easy to source• TO-220 accepts a heatsink • Dropout of about 2 V at 1 A• Quiescent current of about 8 mA• Dissipates (9 V − 5 V) × load, about 2.6 W at my worst case, so a heatsink is required (see the Power Budget)• About 50 °C/W without a heatsink Option 2. TI LM2940CT-5.0 low-dropout 5 V regulator, TO-220$1.94 eachDigi-Key product page · TI datasheet • Dropout of about 1 V at 1 A• Up to 26 V input• Same TO-220 package • About three times the cost of the L7805CV• Higher quiescent current (about 15 mA)• Dissipates the same heat from a 9 V input, so the lower dropout gains nothing• Output capacitor requirements are stricter

Choice: Option 1, L7805CV [Power subsystem]

Rationale: The input is a regulated 9 V adapter, so low dropout buys nothing. The L7805CV is the lowest-cost, most forgiving choice, and its built-in protection suits a board that drives a motor. The heat is the main issue: with the motor on the 5 V rail the regulator dissipates about 2.6 W in the worst case, so the TO-220 needs a small heatsink of about 20 °C/W or better (the Power Budget page shows the calculation).

docs.title: 2.6 [Power subsystem] External 9 V power source
docs.text:
USB power packs are not allowed for this project, so all options are wall adapters. I already own a 9 V 1 A adapter, so it costs nothing new.

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. 9 V 1 A regulated adapter, 5.5 × 2.1 mm, center-positive (equivalent to the Adafruit unit; I already own one)$8.95 if bought new; $0 for meAdafruit product page • Regulated output• Polarity and barrel size are stated• Already owned, so no budget spent• 1 A covers my worst-case need with margin (see the Power Budget) • About 332 mA of spare current after the 25% margin in normal operation, but only about 24 mA in a motor fault unless the DRV8833 current limit is lowered (see the Power Budget)• No room for added loads Option 2. Pololu 9 V 1 A regulated adapter, 5.5 × 2.1 mm, center-positive$11.11 eachPololu product page • Regulated, polarity stated• Light, small body • Same 1 A capacity• More expensive and would use new budget Option 3. SparkFun 9 V 2 A regulated adapter, 5.5 × 2.1 mm$10.95 eachSparkFun product page • 2 A leaves large margin• Regulated • Plug polarity is not stated on the product page• Costs $10.95 of the board's $17.50 to $20.00 share• More than my design needs

Choice: Option 1, my existing 9 V 1 A adapter [Power subsystem]

Rationale: The Power Budget shows the system needs about 0.67 A including the 25% margin, which the 1 A adapter covers. It is already owned, so it uses none of the board's budget, and its polarity is known to be center-positive. In a motor fault the limit matters: the DRV8833 current limit should be set to about 0.67 A rather than the 1 A in my Block Diagram page, otherwise a fault could exceed the adapter's rating.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This schematic is my individual subsystem board, drawn in KiCad 10. It follows my Block Diagram, Component Selection and Power Budget pages. The board takes a position command from Preston's hub board over the ribbon cable. It drives Linear Actuator B (an N20 lead-screw gearmotor) through a DRV8833 H-bridge, closes the loop with a slide potentiometer, and reads an LIS3DH accelerometer for jerk / impulse sensing. Status and IMU data go back to the hub over UART.

  • Power: a 9–12 V barrel jack feeds a removable 1 A fuse and a 1N5819 reverse-polarity diode. Two through-hole linear regulators share the C1/C2 input capacitors:

    • L7805CV, 5 V logic rail: powers the Curiosity Nano and the green power LED.
    • L7806CV, 6 V motor rail: powers only the DRV8833 and the N20 motor, which is rated 6 V.

    The Curiosity Nano's on-board regulator (VTG) supplies 3.3 V to the IMU, the op-amp and the potentiometer. Only the motor and its driver run above 5 V; everything else is 5 V or 3.3 V. The raw 9–12 V reaches only the two regulator inputs. * Controller: the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, drawn as a custom symbol with my initials (KG). It is fed from 5 V through jumper JP1 and Schottky diode D3, so the Nano's USB 5 V cannot back-feed the board's 5 V rail. There are 0.1 µF bypass capacitors on VBUS and VTG. * Actuator with driver circuit: a DRV8833, powered from the 6 V rail through JP2, drives the motor from AIN1/AIN2 (RC2, RD0 PWM), with nSLEEP (RD1) and nFAULT (RB1). The 0.33 Ω sense resistor sets the chopping current limit at about 0.61 A, which stays within the 1 A adapter even in a fault. D6–D9 clamp the motor's back-EMF to VM and GND. JP2 isolates the 6 V motor rail for debugging. * Current-sense signal conditioning: a 159 Hz RC low-pass and an MCP601 non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 11 turn the 0–0.2 V sense voltage into 0–2.2 V for the ADC (RA0). A 1.6 kHz anti-alias filter follows the amplifier. * Sensor: an LIS3DHTR on SPI1 (RC3 SCK, RC4 SDI, RC5 SDO, RD4 CS), with INT1 data-ready on RB0. The slide potentiometer (off-board, on J7) is filtered and read on RA1. * Team interface: a 2x4 IDC header with pin 1 = UART RX (RC7) from the hub, pin 2 = UART TX (RC6) to the hub, and pin 8 = GND. Pins 3–7 are broken out on J3. * Debug and expansion: two debug LEDs (RD2, RD3), a hardware-debounced push button (RD5), 13 bare PCB test pads, and two 13-pin spare GPIO headers that bring out every unused Nano I/O pin.

Figure 1: Driver Nano 3 subsystem schematic (click to enlarge, or open the PDF below for full resolution).

docs.title: Budget choices
docs.text:
The team budget is $70–80 for four boards (about $17.50–20.00 per board; see Component Selection). The schematic keeps costs down where it can:

  • Test points: bare PCB pads cost nothing, instead of about $0.35 each for purchased test points.
  • Headers and jumpers: all are cut from one 40-pin break-away strip.
  • Heatsink: the L7805CV now carries only the Nano and the LED (about 0.1 A), so it needs no heatsink. Only the L7806CV, which carries the motor current, may need the small TO-220 heatsink at 12 V input.

New items compared with Component Selection: the L7806CV, the MCP601-I/P, the 41FR33E sense resistor (the most expensive passive) and six 1N5819 diodes, about $4–5 in total. Passives and headers should come from lab stock where possible, and the totals should be rechecked against current DigiKey prices on the BOM page.

docs.title: Design checks
docs.text:
• ERC: KiCad ERC passes with 0 errors and 1 warning. The warning is the DRV8833's unused bridge-B sense pin (BISEN, bidirectional) tied to GND, where the GND PWR_FLAG sits; this is expected.
  • Capacitor voltage margin (at least 25%): 50 V ceramics on every rail; 47 µF / 25 V on 9–12 V; 10 µF / 25 V electrolytics and the 2.2 µF / 25 V VINT ceramic on 5 V and lower.
  • Test pads: TP1–TP13 are bare PCB pads, so they are not in the BOM.
  • Through-hole parts: every component is through-hole except the DRV8833PWPR (HTSSOP-16) and the LIS3DHTR (LGA-16). Neither comes in a through-hole package; both were accepted on my Component Selection page.
  • Resistor power margin (at least 50%): sense resistor 0.61² × 0.33 = 0.12 W, rated 1 W. All other resistors dissipate less than 10 mW and are rated 1/4 W.
  • Unused inputs: DRV8833 BIN1/BIN2 and the LIS3DH ADC1–3 inputs are pulled down through 10k. LIS3DH CS has a 10k pull-up and DRV8833 nSLEEP a 10k pull-down, so both stay in a safe state while the MCU is in reset.

docs.text:

  2. Update the Power Budget for the new 6 V motor rail (L7806CV), and check whether it needs a heatsink at 12 V: about (12 − 6) V × 0.42 A ≈ 2.5 W at stall.
  3. Copy the part list below into the BOM page with prices.
  4. Breadboard the DRV8833 current-sense amplifier and confirm the gain and the stall threshold with the real motor.

docs.title: Power architecture
docs.text:
• One external source: my own 9 V wall adapter (1 A) on the barrel jack, through a 1 A fuse.
  • Two rails: 9 V (raw adapter voltage, feeding only the regulator) and 5 V (L7805CV linear regulator).
  • The 5 V rail powers the DRV8833 motor supply (VM), the N20 gearmotor, and the Curiosity Nano (VBUS pin).
  • The Curiosity Nano makes its own 3.3 V (VTG), which powers the LIS3DH and the slide-potentiometer reference. That load is counted on the 5 V rail because the Nano's regulator draws it from the 5 V input.

docs.title: Section C. Regulator or source choice per rail
docs.text:
Rail Choice Rationale 5 V ST L7805CV (TO-220) with heatsink Specified for 7 to 18 V input, so the 9 V adapter has 4 V of headroom over its 2 V dropout. Rated up to 1.5 A against a 0.66 A load with margin. Has internal current limiting and thermal shutdown. Compared with the LM2940CT-5.0 in the Component Selection page. 9 V Straight from the wall adapter Only feeds the regulator, so no second regulator is needed

Regulator thermal check:

Quantity Value Load current including margin 657.5 mA Regulator quiescent current (datasheet, about 8 mA) × 1.25 10 mA Power dissipated: (9 V − 5 V) × 0.6575 A 2.63 W Junction rise at 50 °C/W (TO-220, no heatsink) about 131 °C, so it would hit thermal shutdown Junction-to-ambient resistance needed to stay under 125 °C at 40 °C ambient 32 °C/W or lower

The regulator therefore needs a heatsink. Junction-to-case is about 5 °C/W, so a small TO-220 clip-on heatsink of about 20 °C/W or better is enough. At the nominal motor load without margin the dissipation is still about 2.1 W, so the heatsink is needed in normal operation too. This matches the "small heatsink" on my Block Diagram page; it should be sized to this calculation.

docs.title: Section D. External power source
docs.text:
Item Value Source choice My existing 9 V 1 A regulated wall adapter Current into the L7805CV input: (526 + 8) × 1.25 667.5 mA Total required from adapter 667.5 mA Adapter capacity 1000 mA Total remaining current available 332.5 mA (not negative)

This check covers normal operation, where the motor stalls at about 420 mA. The DRV8833 current limit in my Block Diagram page is about 1 A (a 0.2 Ω sense resistor). In a fault the motor could then draw up to 1 A, giving (1000 + 114) × 1.25 = 1,393 mA from the adapter, which is more than it can supply. The limit should be lowered: a sense resistor of about 0.3 Ω gives a limit near 0.67 A, which gives 976 mA from the adapter and keeps the remaining current positive (about 24 mA) even in a fault.

docs.title: Section E. Battery life
docs.text: Not applicable. The design runs from a wall adapter and has no battery.

docs.title: Open items before the design review
docs.text:
1. Measure the stall current of the N20 motor at 5 V and compare it with the 420 mA datasheet figure.
  2. Change the DRV8833 sense resistor from 0.2 Ω to about 0.3 Ω so the current limit is near 0.67 A, and update the Block Diagram page.
  3. Choose and price a small TO-220 heatsink of about 20 °C/W or better. Powering the motor driver from the 9 V rail with the PWM duty capped near 66% (a 6 V motor on 9 V) is an alternative that would remove most of the regulator's heat.
  4. Replace the Nano (100 mA), DRV8833 (5 mA) and LIS3DH (0.5 mA) estimates with measured current.
  5. Copy these numbers into the course power budget spreadsheet template.
